description: Dietary needs for medical conditions, vegetarian and vegan diets, and Halal, Kosher and Hindu requirements.
content_html:
Why Diets Need to Change

A single “standard healthy eating” meal plan cannot meet the needs of every person. Medical diagnoses, ethical choices and religious beliefs all create specific dietary requirements that a food-competent person must be able to plan around. This lesson covers three overlapping groups: those with medical dietary needs or nutritional deficiencies, those who have made lifestyle choices such as vegetarianism or veganism, and those whose religious observances shape what they eat. In your exam, you may be given a scenario featuring any one of these individuals and asked to plan a meal, modify a recipe or evaluate a diet — so knowing the specific requirements in each category is essential.

Medical Conditions and Nutritional Deficiencies

Coeliac Disease

Coeliac disease is an autoimmune condition triggered by gluten — the protein found in wheat, barley and rye. When a person with coeliac disease eats gluten, their immune system attacks the lining of the small intestine, damaging the villi that absorb nutrients. This leads not only to digestive symptoms but also to malabsorption of iron, calcium and B vitamins. The only treatment is a strict, lifelong gluten-free diet: replacing wheat flour with rice flour, cornflour, buckwheat or certified gluten-free alternatives. A student baking a sponge cake for a coeliac friend would substitute gluten-free self-raising flour and check that all other ingredients (including baking powder) are certified gluten-free.

Type 2 Diabetes

Type 2 diabetes develops when the body becomes resistant to insulin or cannot produce enough. Insulin is the hormone that moves glucose from the bloodstream into cells. When it fails, blood glucose remains dangerously high after meals. The dietary priorities are: reducing free sugars and refined carbohydrates (white bread, sugary drinks), increasing NSP to slow glucose absorption, choosing lower-glycaemic-index carbohydrates (oats, pulses, wholegrain bread), reducing saturated fat to manage cardiovascular risk, and maintaining a healthy body weight. A person with type 2 diabetes replacing their usual white-rice side dish with brown rice, adding lentils to a curry and choosing water instead of fruit juice is making four evidence-based improvements simultaneously.

Iron Deficiency Anaemia and Cardiovascular Disease

Iron deficiency anaemia occurs when the body lacks sufficient iron to produce adequate haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. Symptoms include fatigue, pallor, shortness of breath and impaired concentration. Dietary management focuses on increasing haem iron (found in red meat, liver, sardines — the most bioavailable form) and non-haem iron (spinach, lentils, fortified cereals) alongside vitamin C-rich foods, which enhance non-haem iron absorption. Tannins in tea and coffee inhibit iron absorption, so a person with anaemia is advised to avoid drinking them with iron-rich meals.

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) — including coronary heart disease (CHD) — is strongly linked to elevated LDL cholesterol, which builds up as plaques (atherosclerosis) on artery walls, narrowing them and raising the risk of heart attack or stroke. High saturated fat intake raises LDL cholesterol. Dietary management involves replacing saturated fats (butter, lard, fatty cuts of meat, hard cheese) with unsaturated fats (olive oil, avocado, oily fish); increasing NSP (which binds cholesterol in the gut and helps excrete it); reducing salt (which raises blood pressure, increasing CVD risk); and limiting free sugars. Liver disease may also affect the body’s ability to process fat-soluble vitamins and cholesterol, requiring additional medical dietary guidance.

Key Fact

The CVD chain: high saturated fat intake → elevated LDL cholesterol → atherosclerosis (plaque build-up on artery walls) → narrowed arteries → raised risk of heart attack or stroke. This chain appears frequently in extended-response questions.

Other Conditions: Obesity, Dental Caries, Calcium Deficiency and Intolerances

Obesity management requires a sustained negative energy balance — consuming fewer calories than expended — achieved through reducing energy-dense foods (high fat, high free sugar) and increasing physical activity, not through extreme restriction. Dental caries (tooth decay) results from sugar-fermenting bacteria producing acid that erodes tooth enamel; the dietary fix is reducing frequency of free sugar consumption, particularly between meals. Calcium deficiency (affecting bone health and increasing risk of osteoporosis) is addressed by increasing dairy products, fortified plant milks, tinned fish with bones and green leafy vegetables. Nut intolerance requires strict avoidance of tree nuts and peanuts (a legume) and vigilant reading of food labels. Lactose intolerance (inability to digest lactose, the sugar in milk) requires either avoidance of dairy or use of lactase enzyme supplements; plant-based milks (soya, oat, almond) are common substitutes, but calcium levels vary and must be checked.

A person with lactose intolerance who switches to almond milk may assume they are getting the same calcium as before. Unfortified almond milk contains very little calcium — far less than cow’s milk (around 120 mg per 100 ml). Fortified soya milk or fortified oat milk can match cow’s milk calcium levels, but always check the label. For someone using plant milk to meet their calcium RDI, choosing a fortified variety is not optional — it is the difference between meeting and missing the requirement. Exam answers should name the fortified alternative and explain why fortification matters.

Vegetarian and Vegan Diets

The spec names three categories of vegetarian diet that must be known precisely. A lacto-ovo vegetarian eats dairy and eggs. A lacto vegetarian eats dairy but not eggs. A vegan avoids all animal products including dairy, eggs and honey. The key nutritional risks increase as animal foods are excluded: protein quality (essential amino acid completeness), vitamin B12 (found almost exclusively in animal products; vegans must supplement or use fortified foods), calcium (if dairy is excluded), iron (non-haem only, less bioavailable), zinc and omega-3 fatty acids (limited plant sources). Protein complementation — combining plant proteins across meals to ensure all nine essential amino acids are present — is particularly relevant for vegans: rice and lentils together provide a complete amino acid profile that neither provides alone.

Key Fact

Three vegetarian categories: lacto-ovo (dairy + eggs allowed), lacto (dairy only), vegan (no animal products). Vegans face the greatest risk of vitamin B12 deficiency because B12 is found almost exclusively in animal-derived foods.

Religious Dietary Requirements

Religious beliefs create clear and consistent dietary requirements that food professionals must understand and respect. The spec specifically names Hindu, Muslim and Jewish dietary rules. These are observed as part of religious life and are not “preferences” — they are obligations for practising adherents.

Muslim dietary law (Halal): Halal means permitted in Arabic. Pork and all pork derivatives (including lard, gelatine from pork) are prohibited. Alcohol is also forbidden, so dishes containing wine, beer or spirits cannot be served. Meat must be slaughtered in a specific way with a blessing. Processed foods require certification to confirm no cross-contamination with haram (forbidden) ingredients. Planning a meal for a Muslim family means ensuring all meat is Halal-certified, that no pork-derived additives are present, and that alcohol is absent from any ingredient including marinades or sauces.

Jewish dietary law (Kosher): Kosher means fit or proper in Hebrew. Pork and shellfish are not permitted. Meat must come from animals that have cloven hooves and chew cud (beef, lamb). Meat and dairy must not be prepared, cooked or eaten together, which has significant kitchen implications — separate utensils, pots, plates and storage areas are required. Fish with fins and scales is permitted; shellfish is not. A Kosher deli sandwich would use either a meat filling or a cheese filling, never both.

Hindu dietary practice: Many Hindus are vegetarian, particularly those following strict observance, because of the principle of ahimsa (non-violence towards living creatures). Beef is forbidden for most Hindus — the cow is a sacred animal. Many also avoid pork. Dairy products (milk, ghee, yoghurt) are widely used and considered pure. Some Hindu communities fast on certain days and avoid particular foods (onion, garlic) for spiritual reasons. A Hindu vegetarian wedding buffet might feature paneer (fresh cheese), lentil dal, vegetable curries, rice and yoghurt-based raita — all consistent with a lacto-vegetarian diet.

A common oversimplification is to assume that all religious dietary laws are the same, or that they simply mean “no meat.” Muslim and Jewish dietary laws both permit certain meats (Halal beef, Kosher beef and lamb) while restricting specific animals (pork, shellfish). Many Hindus eat meat; the restriction is specifically on beef and often pork. The key distinctions to remember for your exam are: Halal = specific slaughter method + no pork + no alcohol; Kosher = no pork or shellfish + meat-dairy separation + specific slaughter method; Hindu = commonly beef-free and often vegetarian, but dairy is embraced. Conflating these loses application marks on scenario questions.
exam_tip_html: The 12-mark Evaluate question on this topic will typically give you a named individual with a specific dietary need and ask you to evaluate how well a proposed diet or menu meets their needs. The most common error is describing the condition or listing foods without ever reaching a judgement. “Evaluate” means make a reasoned qualitative judgement, weighing strengths and weaknesses against a clear criterion. A top-band answer names specific nutrients at risk (e.g. vitamin B12 for a vegan; calcium for a person with lactose intolerance), explains why they are at risk using the cause-and-effect chain, then weighs whether the proposed menu addresses or fails to address each risk — and commits to a final supported judgement. Without that final judgement sentence (e.g. “Overall, the menu partially meets her needs because it addresses iron but fails to provide a reliable source of vitamin B12”), you will be capped in the Secure band.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Medical conditions create specific dietary requirements: coeliac disease requires strict gluten avoidance; type 2 diabetes requires reduced free sugars and refined carbohydrates; CVD requires reduced saturated fat; iron deficiency anaemia requires haem and non-haem iron sources paired with vitamin C.
  • Three vegetarian categories must be known precisely: lacto-ovo (dairy and eggs permitted), lacto (dairy only), vegan (no animal products). Vegans face the greatest B12, calcium and iron risks and must supplement or use fortified foods.
  • Religious dietary requirements are obligations, not preferences. Key rules: Halal (no pork, no alcohol, specific slaughter); Kosher (no pork or shellfish, no meat-dairy mixing); Hindu (commonly beef-free, dairy embraced, many are lacto-vegetarian).

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following conditions requires a strict, lifelong gluten-free diet?
A) Type 2 diabetes
B) Lactose intolerance
C) Coeliac disease
D) Iron deficiency anaemia
Name the three categories of vegetarian diet as defined in the specification.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for all three correct: lacto-ovo vegetarian, lacto vegetarian, vegan. All three must be named for the mark.

practice_questions.text: State two dietary changes a person with type 2 diabetes should make to help manage their blood glucose levels.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct, distinct change, up to 2. Acceptable answers: reduce free sugars or sugary drinks; reduce refined carbohydrates (white bread, white rice, white pasta); increase NSP (slows glucose absorption); choose lower-glycaemic-index carbohydrates (oats, wholegrains, pulses); reduce saturated fat to manage cardiovascular risk; maintain a healthy body weight.

practice_questions.text: Describe the main dietary requirements of a Muslim family observing Halal dietary law.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each distinct, described requirement, up to 3. Acceptable answers: pork and all pork derivatives (including lard, pork-based gelatine) are forbidden; alcohol is forbidden, including in ingredients such as wine-based sauces or marinades; meat must be slaughtered in the Halal way with a blessing; processed foods must be Halal-certified to confirm no cross-contamination with haram (forbidden) ingredients. Credit also: checking food labels for pork-derived additives such as E-numbers derived from lard.

practice_questions.text: Callum has recently been diagnosed with iron deficiency anaemia. Explain how he should change his diet to increase iron absorption, and why each change will help.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for each correct change with a linked explanation, up to 4. Acceptable chains: include more haem iron sources such as red meat and sardines (1) because haem iron is more bioavailable and absorbed more efficiently than plant-based iron (1); include more non-haem iron sources such as spinach, lentils and fortified cereals (1) alongside vitamin C-rich foods such as orange juice or peppers (1) because vitamin C converts non-haem iron to a more absorbable form; avoid drinking tea or coffee with iron-rich meals (1) because tannins in these drinks bind to iron and inhibit its absorption (1). Award a maximum of 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how well a lacto-ovo vegetarian diet can meet the nutritional needs of a 15-year-old girl who has recently given up meat and fish. Consider both the nutrients that are easily met and those at risk of deficiency, and reach a supported judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Detailed evaluation of at least three specific nutrients — both those well covered (protein via eggs and dairy, calcium via dairy, most B vitamins) and those at risk (vitamin B12 limited to eggs and dairy so adequate if consumed; iron present as non-haem only and less bioavailable; zinc; potentially omega-3 from eggs but limited). Specific RDI values or age-related context cited (teenage girl has elevated iron need due to menstruation, elevated calcium need for bone formation). Both sides of the evaluation clearly developed and weighed against each other. Supported judgement present — e.g. 'Overall, a lacto-ovo vegetarian diet can meet most of this student's needs IF dairy and eggs are consumed regularly, but her elevated iron needs due to menstruation make iron deficiency the most significant risk, and pairing non-haem sources with vitamin C foods is essential.' Accurate food-science vocabulary throughout.

Secure (7-9 marks): Most relevant points covered, at least two nutrients analysed from each side, some age-specific context applied, a judgement reached but not fully supported or partially one-sided.

Developing (4-6 marks): Relevant points about vegetarian diets present but analysis limited; may list foods without explaining why nutrients are at risk; judgement attempted but vague or unsupported by evidence.

Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic facts about vegetarian diets; limited application to the named student's age or sex; no judgement or a purely descriptive response listing foods.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is the main dietary treatment for coeliac disease?
Under Jewish Kosher law, which two foods must never be prepared or eaten together?
A lacto-ovo vegetarian eats dairy products and _____ but avoids all meat, poultry and fish.
Vitamin _____ is found almost exclusively in animal products, making it the greatest deficiency risk for vegans.
Match each dietary requirement to the correct group:
left: No pork; no alcohol; specific slaughter method
No pork or shellfish; no meat and dairy together
No beef; dairy embraced; commonly lacto-vegetarian

flashcard_questions.q: What is coeliac disease, and what is its only treatment?
flashcard_questions.a: An autoimmune condition triggered by gluten that damages the small intestine lining. The only treatment is a strict, lifelong gluten-free diet.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the key dietary priorities for someone with type 2 diabetes?
flashcard_questions.a: Reduce free sugars and refined carbohydrates, increase NSP, choose lower-GI foods, reduce saturated fat, and maintain a healthy body weight.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the CVD chain linking saturated fat to heart attack risk?
flashcard_questions.a: High saturated fat intake raises LDL cholesterol, which deposits on artery walls as plaques (atherosclerosis), narrowing arteries and raising the risk of heart attack or stroke.

flashcard_questions.q: Why should iron-rich plant foods be eaten with vitamin C?
flashcard_questions.a: Vitamin C converts non-haem iron to a more absorbable form, significantly increasing the amount of iron the body can absorb.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three categories of vegetarian diet, from least to most restrictive?
flashcard_questions.a: Lacto-ovo vegetarian (dairy and eggs); lacto vegetarian (dairy only); vegan (no animal products at all).

flashcard_questions.q: Why are vegans at greatest risk of vitamin B12 deficiency?
flashcard_questions.a: B12 is found almost exclusively in animal products; vegans must supplement or use fortified foods such as nutritional yeast or fortified plant milks.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Halal mean, and what foods does it prohibit?
flashcard_questions.a: Halal means permitted under Islamic dietary law. Pork and all pork derivatives are forbidden, as is alcohol. Meat must be slaughtered in a specific way.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Kosher mean, and what is a key preparation rule?
flashcard_questions.a: Kosher means fit or proper under Jewish dietary law. Pork and shellfish are forbidden, and meat and dairy must never be prepared, cooked or eaten together.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main beef-related restriction in Hindu dietary practice?
flashcard_questions.a: Most Hindus do not eat beef because the cow is considered a sacred animal. Dairy is widely consumed and considered pure.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two dietary changes to manage obesity.
flashcard_questions.a: Reduce energy-dense foods (high fat, high free sugar) and increase physical activity to achieve a sustained negative energy balance.

flashcard_questions.q: What causes dental caries and what dietary change helps prevent it?
flashcard_questions.a: Bacteria fermenting free sugars produce acid that erodes tooth enamel. Reducing the frequency of free sugar consumption, especially between meals, is the key dietary fix.

glossary_terms.definition: An autoimmune condition in which gluten triggers an immune response that damages the lining of the small intestine.
A protein formed when glutenin and gliadin in wheat flour combine with water; responsible for the elasticity and structure of bread dough.
Conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels, often linked to diets high in saturated fat, salt and free sugars.
A vegetarian who eats dairy products and eggs but avoids all meat, poultry and fish.
A vegetarian who eats dairy products but avoids eggs, meat, poultry and fish.
Someone who avoids all animal products including meat, fish, dairy, eggs and usually honey.
Arabic for 'permitted'; describes food that complies with Islamic dietary law, including requirements for how animals are slaughtered and the prohibition of pork and alcohol.
Hebrew for 'fit'; describes food that complies with Jewish dietary law, including rules on permitted species, slaughter method and the separation of meat and dairy.
The build-up of fatty plaques (largely cholesterol) on artery walls, narrowing the arteries and increasing the risk of heart attack or stroke.

hero_image_caption: Understanding individual dietary needs — whether for medical, lifestyle or religious reasons — is the foundation of good meal planning.
